blocks.text: 1. Hyperparameter Spaces

blocks.alt: A hyperparameter gets a defined range, forming the search space

blocks.text: Grid Search, Random Search, Bayesian Optimization, Optuna, and Early Stopping, every topic covered so far in this module, quietly assumed the hyperparameter search space itself was already well-defined, a reasonable set of candidate values or distributions simply handed to whichever tuning technique was being covered. Hyperparameter Spaces closes this module by examining that assumption directly, since how the search space itself actually gets designed shapes the effectiveness of every single tuning technique built on top of it.

A poorly designed search space, one with the wrong spacing, unreasonable boundaries, or a failure to represent genuine dependencies between hyperparameters, can undermine even the most sophisticated search strategy covered earlier in this module, no matter how cleverly that strategy explores whatever space it was actually given. This closing topic covers exactly how to design a hyperparameter space well.
2. Linear versus Log Spacing, in Full Depth

blocks.alt: Linear spacing is compared against log spacing

blocks.text: Both the Grid Search and Random Search topics briefly previewed a distinction worth returning to in full depth here: some hyperparameters, regularization strength being the clearest example already encountered throughout the Regression and Classification modules, naturally span several orders of magnitude, meaningfully useful values ranging anywhere from 0.0001 up to 100 or beyond.

Linear spacing, evenly spaced candidate values across that entire range, wastes the overwhelming majority of its coverage on one narrow region, since most evenly spaced points between 0.0001 and 100 end up clustered near the larger end of that range, leaving the smaller orders of magnitude badly undersampled. Log spacing, values spaced evenly on a logarithmic scale instead, gives proportionally equal attention to every order of magnitude, 0.0001 to 0.001 gets explored just as thoroughly as 1 to 10, exactly the kind of balanced coverage this specific type of hyperparameter genuinely needs.
3. Recognizing Which Hyperparameters Need Log-Scale Treatment

blocks.alt: A learning rate with a wide range needs log scale

blocks.text: Regularization strength and learning rate, both already covered extensively throughout the Regression, Classification, and Ensemble Learning modules, are the clearest examples of hyperparameters that genuinely need log-scale treatment, since meaningfully different behavior can occur at 0.001 versus 0.01, a tenfold difference that linear spacing would badly under-explore.

Other hyperparameters, like the number of trees in a Random Forest, the maximum depth of a Decision Tree, or K in KNN, all already covered in depth in the Classification module, tend to be naturally meaningful across a comparatively narrow, genuinely linear range, where the difference between 50 and 60 trees matters roughly as much as the difference between 100 and 110 trees, making ordinary linear spacing the more natural, appropriate choice for these specific hyperparameters instead.

blocks.text: 4. Setting Reasonable Range Boundaries

Choosing where a hyperparameter's search range actually starts and ends connects directly back to the bias-variance tradeoff underlying nearly every hyperparameter covered throughout this entire course. Setting a range too narrow risks excluding the true best value entirely, if it happens to sit just outside whatever boundaries were originally chosen, no tuning technique covered earlier in this module can ever find a value that was never included in the search space to begin with.

Setting a range too wide wastes search budget exploring values that are almost certainly too extreme to ever prove useful in practice, values so far toward underfitting or overfitting that no genuinely well-performing model would ever actually use them. A reasonable starting range is typically informed either by existing domain knowledge about the specific algorithm and problem, or by running a quick, cheap preliminary search first, to get a rough sense of where reasonable values are likely to actually sit before committing to a more thorough, expensive search.

blocks.title: tip
blocks.content: A cheap preliminary search, using a small sample budget and a wide, rough range, is a genuinely useful practical technique for narrowing down reasonable boundaries before committing to a more thorough, expensive Grid Search, Random Search, or Bayesian Optimization run.

blocks.text: 5. Representing Conditional Hyperparameters

blocks.alt: A kernel choice determines whether a dependent parameter appears at all

blocks.text: Recall from the Optuna topic that its define-by-run design was built specifically to handle hyperparameters that only exist, or only genuinely matter, given some other hyperparameter's specific value. The number of neighbors, K, is entirely meaningless unless the algorithm actually chosen for a given trial is KNN specifically, exactly the algorithm covered in depth in the Classification module.

Kernel type is similarly meaningless unless the algorithm actually chosen is SVM. A well-designed hyperparameter space represents these genuine dependencies explicitly, rather than pretending every single hyperparameter always applies uniformly regardless of which algorithm or configuration is actually active for a given trial. Failing to represent these dependencies correctly can waste enormous amounts of search budget exploring nonsensical combinations, like tuning K for a trial that is not even using KNN in the first place.
6. Numeric versus Categorical Hyperparameters

blocks.alt: A numeric continuous range is compared against categorical discrete choices

blocks.text: A well-designed hyperparameter space needs to correctly represent several genuinely different types of hyperparameters. Numeric, continuous hyperparameters, learning rate and regularization strength being the clearest examples, are sampled from a genuine range of real-numbered values. Numeric, integer hyperparameters, the number of trees or maximum tree depth being clear examples, are sampled from whole numbers only, never a fractional value like 47.3 trees.

Categorical hyperparameters, kernel type or solver algorithm being clear examples, are instead chosen from a fixed, discrete list of distinct options with no inherent numeric ordering between them at all, RBF, linear, and polynomial kernels are simply different choices, not points along a continuous numeric scale. Correctly representing each hyperparameter as the right one of these three types is essential for every tuning technique covered earlier in this module to search the space sensibly.
7. Encoding Prior Knowledge into the Space

blocks.alt: Domain knowledge produces a narrower, smarter search space

blocks.text: It is worth connecting this back to Bayesian Optimization's core probabilistic philosophy, already covered in depth in its own topic, since a well-designed search space can itself encode existing knowledge before any actual search even begins, in a sense complementary to how the surrogate model refines its own knowledge as the search progresses.

Centering a hyperparameter's range around values that have commonly proven effective on similar problems in the past, based on prior experience or published benchmarks, gives whatever tuning technique gets applied a genuinely useful head start, reducing how much that technique has to discover essentially from scratch. This is not a strict guarantee of finding the true optimum faster, but it is a genuinely useful practical habit, directly complementing whichever specific tuning technique, Grid Search, Random Search, or Bayesian Optimization, ultimately gets applied on top of this thoughtfully designed space.

blocks.text: 8. Why This Benefits Every Technique in This Module

It is worth stating directly, closing out this topic, exactly why a well-designed search space matters so universally. Grid Search's combinatorial explosion, already covered in its own topic, gets meaningfully worse when the search space is unnecessarily large or poorly spaced. Random Search's fixed sample budget, already covered in its own topic, gets spent less efficiently when that budget has to cover an unnecessarily large, poorly designed space.

This limitation is not specific to any one single tuning technique; every technique covered throughout this entire module, Grid Search, Random Search, Bayesian Optimization, and Optuna, all ultimately share this same underlying dependency on the quality of the underlying search space they are given to work with. This makes designing the hyperparameter space thoughtfully, exactly the practices covered throughout this topic, the one single improvement that genuinely benefits literally every tuning technique covered in this module equally, regardless of which specific one ultimately gets applied.
9. A Practical Workflow for Designing a Search Space

Putting everything covered throughout this topic together into one practical, repeatable workflow: first, identify which hyperparameters genuinely matter for the specific algorithm being tuned, rather than including every conceivable hyperparameter indiscriminately. Second, choose linear or log spacing for each one individually, based on how that specific hyperparameter naturally behaves, exactly the distinction covered in depth earlier in this topic.

Third, set reasonable range boundaries for each hyperparameter, informed by domain knowledge or a cheap preliminary search. Fourth, represent any genuine conditional dependencies between hyperparameters explicitly, rather than treating every hyperparameter as if it always applies uniformly. Only after these four steps have been worked through thoughtfully should Grid Search, Random Search, or Bayesian Optimization, whichever specific technique best fits the situation according to their own respective topics, actually be applied on top of this well-designed foundation.
10. Worked Example
The example below defines a well-designed hyperparameter space for a Gradient Boosting classifier, correctly applying log spacing, linear spacing, and categorical choices together.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import loguniform, randint
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV, train_test_split

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(300, 4))
y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] * 0.5 + rng.normal(scale=0.8, size=300) > 0).astype(int)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

# A well-designed space: log spacing for learning rate, linear (integer) for tree
# count and depth, categorical for the splitting criterion
param_distributions = {
    'learning_rate': loguniform(0.001, 0.3),   # spans orders of magnitude: log spacing
    'n_estimators': randint(50, 300),           # a narrow, naturally linear range
    'max_depth': randint(2, 6),                 # a narrow, naturally linear range
    'criterion': ['friedman_mse', 'squared_error'],  # categorical, fixed discrete choices
}

search = RandomizedSearchCV(
    GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=42),
    param_distributions,
    n_iter=30, cv=5, random_state=42
)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f"Best combination found: {search.best_params_}")
print(f"Best cross validation score: {search.best_score_:.3f}")
print(f"Test set score: {search.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Notice learning_rate uses loguniform, exactly the log-spacing treatment this topic covers for hyperparameters spanning orders of magnitude, while n_estimators and max_depth use randint, ordinary linear sampling appropriate for their naturally narrow, linear ranges.

blocks.text: 11. Hyperparameter Tuning Module Complete

blocks.alt: The Hyperparameter Tuning module is complete, Probability-Based Models comes next

blocks.text: This closes the Hyperparameter Tuning module, six topics building a complete toolkit for choosing good hyperparameters: Grid Search's exhaustive but combinatorially limited approach, Random Search's efficient random sampling, Bayesian Optimization's intelligent use of past results, Optuna's practical, production-ready implementation, Early Stopping's generalized protection against overfitting during training itself, and finally Hyperparameter Spaces' treatment of the foundation every one of those techniques actually searches over.

Every technique in this module builds directly on the Cross Validation module's foundation from before it, using K-Fold or Nested Cross Validation to evaluate candidate hyperparameter settings honestly. The next module, Probability-Based Models, shifts focus to a different family of algorithms entirely, ones built around explicit probabilistic reasoning as their core mechanism, rather than the search-and-tune workflow that has occupied the last several modules.
12. Key Takeaways

items: Hyperparameter Spaces examines how the search space itself gets designed, the foundation every tuning technique in this module builds on.
Hyperparameters spanning orders of magnitude, like regularization strength, need log spacing; narrower, linear ones use linear spacing.
Range boundaries that are too narrow can exclude the true best value; too wide wastes budget on almost certainly useless extremes.
A well-designed space represents genuine conditional dependencies between hyperparameters explicitly, not as if every one always applies.
It must correctly distinguish continuous numeric, integer numeric, and categorical hyperparameters.
Centering ranges around commonly effective prior values gives any tuning technique a genuinely useful head start.
An unnecessarily large or poorly designed space wastes computational budget regardless of which tuning technique gets applied.
A practical workflow: identify relevant hyperparameters, choose spacing, set boundaries, represent dependencies, then tune.
This closes the Hyperparameter Tuning module; next up: Probability-Based Models, shifting to algorithms built around explicit probabilistic reasoning.
